concepts.name: Constitutional vs. Statutory Status of Lokpal
key_dimensions: Lokpal is a statutory body under the Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act, 2013 — NOT a constitutional body (common trap)
Comparison with CAG and Election Commission which have constitutional backing under Articles 148 and 324
Implications of statutory vs. constitutional status on independence, removal, and jurisdiction
Contrast with Lokayuktas — some states have constitutional provisions (e.g., Maharashtra) while others rely on statutes

concepts.name: Composition and Structure of Lokpal
key_dimensions: Chairperson + maximum 8 members (50% judicial, 50% non-judicial — exact ratio is a frequent MCQ trap)
50% of members must belong to SC/ST/OBC/minorities/women — mandatory diversity clause
Distinction between 'judicial member' (served as SC judge or HC Chief Justice) and 'non-judicial member' qualifications
Lokpal as a multi-member body vs. single Ombudsman in many countries — significance for institutional design

concepts.name: Appointment Process and Selection Committee
key_dimensions: Selection Committee composition: PM (Chairperson), Lok Sabha Speaker, Leader of Opposition in LS, CJI or nominee, one eminent jurist
Role of the Search Committee in preparing a panel — 8 members, 50% from SC/ST/OBC/minorities/women
Trap: Leader of Opposition vs. Leader of single largest opposition party when no formal LoP exists
Absence of LoP in 16th and 17th Lok Sabha and its impact on Lokpal appointments — constitutional controversy

concepts.name: Tenure, Removal, and Service Conditions of Lokpal
key_dimensions: Term: 5 years or until age 70, whichever is earlier — not eligible for reappointment
Removal: President acts on an inquiry by Supreme Court — parallels with removal of SC judges but distinct process
Grounds for removal: misbehavior, incapacity — proven after SC inquiry (not impeachment by Parliament)
Salary and service conditions charged to Consolidated Fund of India — significance for financial independence

concepts.name: Jurisdiction of Lokpal: Who Falls Under Its Purview
key_dimensions: Covers PM, Union Ministers, MPs, Group A/B/C/D officers, and employees of bodies financed by Central Government
Critical trap: PM is covered but with significant restrictions/exclusions (security, integrity, relations with foreign states, etc.)
NGOs receiving donations above a threshold from foreign/government sources are covered — recent expansion
Exclusion of judiciary (HC and SC judges covered under separate mechanisms like in-house procedure)

concepts.name: Special Protections and Restrictions on Complaints Against the Prime Minister
key_dimensions: Complaints against PM excluded in matters of international relations, external and internal security, public order, atomic energy, and space
Lokpal can investigate PM only if full bench (all members) sits and 2/3rd majority approves proceeding
Inquiry against PM must be held in camera — unique procedural safeguard
If Lokpal finds no case, all records must be destroyed — protection against misuse and political targeting

concepts.name: Jurisdiction Over Members of Parliament: Article 105 Overlap
key_dimensions: Parliamentary privilege under Article 105(2) protects MPs for votes and speeches inside Parliament
Lokpal cannot investigate MPs for corruption related to votes/speech in Parliament — constitutional shield
Trap: This doesn't mean MPs are fully exempt — acts outside Parliament (e.g., bribery to vote) are covered
Comparison with P V Narasimha Rao case (1998) where SC upheld immunity — pending reconsideration by larger bench

concepts.name: Inquiry and Investigation Powers of Lokpal
key_dimensions: Two-stage process: Preliminary Inquiry by Lokpal (to ascertain prima facie case) → Investigation by CBI or its own Investigation Wing
Lokpal can direct CBI to investigate — but cannot supervise CBI in cases not referred by it (important distinction)
Power to attach property during investigation under Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988
Time limits: Preliminary inquiry within 30 days (extendable to 6 months); Investigation within 6 months (extendable to 1 year)

concepts.name: Lokpal's Relationship with CBI: Superintendence and Control
key_dimensions: Lokpal has superintendence over CBI for cases referred by it — not general superintendence (trap: that belongs to DSPE Act/MHA)
CBI Director appointment: DSPE Act amended to involve PM, LoP, and CJI — separate from but connected to Lokpal framework
Lokpal's approval needed before CBI can close cases referred by it or transfer investigating officers in such cases
Tension between Lokpal's oversight and CBI's functional autonomy — structural ambiguity in the Act

concepts.name: Prosecution and Adjudication: Special Courts and Trial Process
key_dimensions: Lokpal can recommend prosecution to Special Courts established under the Act or designated by Central Government
Sanction for prosecution of public servants: Lokpal itself is the sanctioning authority (replacing the traditional executive sanction) — key reform
Trial must be completed within 2 years (extendable in 6-month blocks by Special Court with recorded reasons)
Acquittal doesn't automatically protect against departmental proceedings — dual track accountability

concepts.name: Protection Against False and Frivolous Complaints
key_dimensions: Complainant can be penalized if complaint is false: fine up to ₹1 lakh and/or imprisonment up to 1 year
Lokpal must hear the complainant before imposing penalty — principle of natural justice embedded
Balance between encouraging whistleblowing and discouraging motivated/vexatious complaints — policy tension
Comparison with Whistleblowers Protection Act, 2014 — different but complementary mechanism

concepts.name: Asset Disclosure Norms Under Lokpal Framework
key_dimensions: Public servants (Group A, B, C, D) required to declare assets and liabilities of themselves, spouse, and dependent children
Annual filing mandated — Lokpal has oversight role in ensuring compliance
Non-compliance and false declarations are grounds for inquiry and prosecution under the Act
Trap: Asset disclosure under Lokpal Act is different from election affidavit disclosure under RPA — different purposes and enforcement

concepts.name: Lokayukta: Constitutional Mandate and State-Level Variation
key_dimensions: Lokpal Act 2013 mandates states to establish Lokayuktas within 1 year — but no penalty for non-compliance (weak enforcement)
Second ARC (2005) recommendation for a uniform model — not implemented; wide variation across states
States with strong Lokayuktas: Karnataka (oldest, 1984 amendment model), Maharashtra; states yet to establish effective ones
Trap: Lokpal Act doesn't prescribe a uniform structure for Lokayuktas — states have legislative freedom under Entry 1, List II

concepts.name: Karnataka Lokayukta: Model and Significance
key_dimensions: Considered the most effective Lokayukta — has suo motu powers, can register FIR directly (unlike many state counterparts)
Empowered to investigate CM, Ministers, MLAs, and state government employees
Karnataka Lokayukta Act 1984 — landmark in anti-corruption architecture at state level
Controversy: ACB vs. Lokayukta jurisdiction in Karnataka — political attempts to dilute Lokayukta powers

concepts.name: Lokpal vs. CVC: Overlapping Jurisdiction and Differentiation
key_dimensions: CVC is an advisory body — can only recommend; Lokpal has prosecutorial and quasi-judicial powers (key distinction)
CVC covers Group A officers and above for vigilance matters; Lokpal has broader jurisdiction including political executives
CVC set up by CVC Act 2003 (statutory); earlier only executive resolution (1964) — compare with Lokpal's 2013 statute
Trap: Both can look at CBI but in different capacities — CVC has general superintendence over CBI; Lokpal only for referred cases

concepts.name: Historical Evolution: From First ARC to Lokpal Act 2013
key_dimensions: First Administrative Reforms Commission (1966) under Morarji Desai first recommended Lokpal — 8 failed bills before 2013
Anna Hazare movement (2011) and Jan Lokpal Bill demand vs. Government's Lokpal Bill — key differences in scope and independence
Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act passed December 2013, operationalized only in 2019 (first Lokpal appointed March 2019) — long gap
Successive Parliamentary Standing Committee recommendations and their incorporation — evolution of the institutional design

concepts.name: Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988 and Its Amendment (2018) — Interface with Lokpal
key_dimensions: 2018 amendment introduced the offence of 'bribe-giving' (not just receiving) — demand not necessary for conviction
Prior sanction for prosecution now required even for retired public servants — expanded protection (trap: earlier only serving officers)
Lokpal Act and PC Act work in tandem — Lokpal is the sanctioning authority for Group A officers, replacing executive
Definition of 'public servant' under PC Act is wider than Lokpal's jurisdiction — important boundary condition

concepts.name: Lokpal's Powers Compared with Ombudsman Models Globally
key_dimensions: Swedish Ombudsman (oldest, 1809) — purely investigative, no prosecutorial power; Lokpal has both investigative and quasi-judicial powers
UK Parliamentary Commissioner for Administration — investigates only on MP referral; Lokpal accepts direct complaints
Hong Kong ICAC model — integrated investigation and prosecution; India deliberately separated CBI from Lokpal to avoid concentration
UPSC relevance: India's hybrid model — arguments for and against giving Lokpal suo motu powers (currently absent)

concepts.name: Suo Motu Powers: Absence and Implications
key_dimensions: Lokpal cannot take suo motu cognizance — can only act on complaints (major criticism and contrast with some Lokayuktas)
Complainant must be a person (individual, society, trust) — anonymous complaints not entertained directly
Contrast: CAG, NHRC, and some High Courts have suo motu jurisdiction — institutional design choice with accountability implications
Debate: Granting suo motu powers risks political misuse vs. denial limits proactive anti-corruption action

concepts.name: Lokpal and Federalism: Centre-State Tension
key_dimensions: Anti-corruption for state public servants is a State subject (Entry 1, List II) — Lokpal's direct jurisdiction is limited to central public servants

Mandate to establish Lokayuktas under the central Act raises questions of legislative competence — justified under Concurrent List Entry 13 (civil services) and Article 253 (international obligations via UNCAC)
UNCAC (UN Convention Against Corruption) ratified by India 2011 — provided international law basis for central legislation
States argue that uniform Lokayukta structure imposed by Centre violates federal spirit — ongoing tension
